examples.question_text: A prism has a uniform cross-sectional area of $14\text{ cm}^{2}$ and a volume of $119\text{ cm}^{3}$. Find the distance $h$ between its parallel cross-sections.
A prism has a volume of $102\text{ mm}^{3}$. The distance between its parallel cross-sections is $6\text{ mm}$. Find the area $A$ of its uniform cross-section.

examples.solution_text:
Use the $7\text{ cm}$ by $4\text{ cm}$ face as the cross-section.
$\begin{align*}A &= 7\times4\\&=28\text{ cm}^{2}\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}V &= Ax\\168 &=28x\\x &=\frac{168}{28}\\x &=6\text{ cm}\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A cube has a volume of $200\text{ cm}^{3}$. Find its side length $x$, correct to $2$ decimal places.
Two rectangular prisms have the same volume. Prism A has dimensions $x\text{ cm}$, $5\text{ cm}$ and $3\text{ cm}$. Prism B has dimensions $8\text{ cm}$, $6\text{ cm}$ and $5\text{ cm}$. Find $x$.
examples.solution_text:
Prism B:
$\begin{align*}V &= (8\times6)\times5\\&=240\text{ cm}^{3}\end{align*}$
Prism A:
$\begin{align*}A &=5\times3\\&=15\text{ cm}^{2}\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}V &=Ax\\240 &=15x\\x &=\frac{240}{15}\\x &=16\text{ cm}\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A rectangular prism measures $16\text{ cm}$ by $9\text{ cm}$ by $5\text{ cm}$. Its volume is double the volume of a cube with side length $x\text{ cm}$. Find $x$, correct to $2$ decimal places.
examples.solution_text:
Rectangular prism:
$\begin{align*}V &=(16\times9)\times5\\&=720\text{ cm}^{3}\end{align*}$
The cube has half this volume.
$\begin{align*}V_{\text{cube}} &=720\div2\\&=360\text{ cm}^{3}\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}360 &=x^{3}\\x &=\sqrt[3]{360}\\&=7.1137\ldots\\&\approx7.11\text{ cm}\end{align*}$

coverage.summary: Authored six examples covering all six distinct accepted assessment methods, using different values and supplied booklet methods. All 33 assessment locators are mapped without re-auditing or altering assessments. Questions and solutions are separate; editable solution prose and mathematics inherit renderer blue. Working uses aligned relation gutters, and the rectangular-prism diagram retains black labels, explicit faces and view-based hidden edges. Independent example review and final-size capture remain pending.

examples.derivation: 119 = 14h, so h = 119/14 = 8.5 cm. This follows the supplied missing-length exercise.
102 = 6A, so A = 102/6 = 17 mm². Image25(b) supports finding an unknown cross-sectional area.
The known rectangular cross-section has area 7 × 4 = 28 cm². Therefore 168 = 28x and x = 6 cm. The diagram places x along the distance between these cross-sections.
x³ = 200 gives the positive root x = 5.848035… cm, which rounds to 5.85 cm. Source cube-dimension exercises support this method.
Prism B has volume 8 × 6 × 5 = 240 cm³. Prism A has known cross-sectional area 5 × 3 = 15 cm², giving x = 240/15 = 16 cm. This matches the equal-volume method in source Q4.
The rectangular prism has volume 16 × 9 × 5 = 720 cm³. The cube has volume 360 cm³, so x = ∛360 = 7.113786… cm, rounding to 7.11 cm. This matches source Q5's double-volume relationship.
